interactive.title: Two brackets and their product
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on solving a quadratic equation from its two brackets. A pointer sits on a number line for x, and on the screens that show an idea you slide it yourself, in steps of 0.5. Above it are three bars: the value of the first bracket, the value of the second bracket, and their product, each rising from a zero line when it is above zero and hanging below when it is below zero. One pointer feeds both brackets, because both hold the same x; a bracket that is just x is labelled x alone, so it is not read as the pointer. Below the bars, a dot rides the curve of the quadratic, a sketch drawn from its rule: the dot's height is the product, so the dot sits on the x-axis exactly when the product bar is at zero. On the first screen the brackets are x − 2 and x − 5 and x runs from −1 to 8. Each later screen sets its own brackets and its own stretch of x, such as x + 2 and x + 5, or x and x − 6, or x + 3 and x − 3. On screen 5 a switch changes the equation from = 0 to = 10, and a line at height 10 crosses the graph, so you can see where the product is 10 and read off both bars there. On screen 11 both bars are x − 3, so they reach zero together and the curve only touches the axis. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to pick one answer from three. On screen 10 the first bar is 3x. Screen 6 shows a worked wrong answer for you to find the slip, and screen 14 solves the box from Calculus fundamentals. A wrong pick puts its numbers back into the equation and shows what they make, next to what the equation needs; when its x lies off the pointer's line, a note says so and the bars stay where they were.
interactive.ignores: The curve is drawn only over the stretch of x on screen; these parabolas carry on rising either side for ever. The product bar is drawn to its own scale, smaller than the bracket bars, so only its sign and its zero can be compared with them, not its length. Any bar whose value is not zero is drawn at least a few pixels tall, so only a value of exactly 0 is flat. The pointer moves in steps of 0.5, so it lands exactly on these roots because they were chosen to be whole numbers; a root between steps would be passed over, usually with the product changing sign on either side of it. Every quadratic here was chosen to factorise with whole numbers. Many do not, and lessons 4 and 5 find their roots another way, where they have them.

explain.text:
Factorising pays off when a quadratic is set equal to zero. It turns the quadratic into two brackets multiplied together, and if the product of two numbers is zero then one or both of them must be zero.[^1] So each bracket can be set to zero on its own, and (x − 2)(x − 5) = 0 gives x = 2 or x = 5.

Here is why a zero product needs a zero factor. Say a × b = 0 and a is not zero. Then you can divide both sides by a, as in Solving equations, and b = 0 ÷ a, which is 0. So if one factor is not zero, the other must be. On the picture, one pointer feeds both brackets, because both hold the same x. At x = 3 the bars read 1 and −2, and the product is −2. At x = 2 the x − 2 bar is 0, so the product is 0 even though the other bar reads −3, and at x = 5 it is the x − 5 bar's turn. Values of x that make an equation true are its [[root]]s, a different job from the square roots of Powers and roots, so this equation has two roots, 2 and 5. Each bracket is zero at the number that cancels it, so the root has the opposite sign to the number in its bracket: x + 2 is zero at x = −2, and (x + 2)(x + 5) = 0 gives x = −2 or x = −5. The dot rides the graph of y = (x − 2)(x − 5), the U-shaped parabola from Functions and their graphs.[^2] Its height is the product, and on the axis the height is zero, so the dot meets the axis exactly at the two roots.

The rule needs a zero on one side. If (x − 2)(x − 5) = 10, the product is 10 at x = 0, where the brackets are −2 and −5, and at x = 7, where they are 5 and 2, so neither bracket is 10. Two numbers can multiply to 10 in endlessly many ways, so a 10 says nothing about either bracket alone, and x − 2 = 10 gives x = 12, where the product is 10 × 7 = 70. Move the 10 across first: x² − 7x + 10 = 10, so x² − 7x = 0, which is x(x − 7) = 0, and x = 0 or x = 7. Dividing both sides by x is safe only when x cannot be 0, and x = 0 is exactly the root it throws away: x² = 6x divided by x leaves x = 6 alone, but taking 6x across gives x(x − 6) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 6. Dividing by a number such as 3 is fine, since 3 is never 0, so 3x² = 48 becomes x² = 16.

An equation such as x² = 9 has two roots, because a negative number times itself is positive too. x² = 9 becomes x² − 9 = 0, the difference of two squares from lesson 2, so (x + 3)(x − 3) = 0 and x = 3 or x = −3, written x = ±3. A perfect square set to zero has one root: x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)² = 0 only at x = 3, where both brackets are zero together. The square of any number on the number line is never below zero, so that parabola reaches the axis at 3 and turns back up without crossing. The brackets themselves are not the answer: (x + 4)(x − 3) is x² + x − 12 factorised, and the roots of x² + x − 12 = 0 are −4 and 3. Put each root back to check it, because a slip in the brackets gives roots that fail. Lessons 4 and 5 deal with quadratics that have no whole-number pair.

**If a product is zero, at least one of its factors is zero,[^1] so get zero on one side, factorise, and set each bracket to zero: (x − 2)(x − 5) = 0 gives x = 2 or x = 5.**

analogy.text: Think of two switches in series feeding a lamp, with the supply on and the lamp sound. The lamp is dark only if at least one switch is open, just as a product is zero only if at least one bracket is zero. So to find every way the lamp goes dark you test each switch on its own, as you set each bracket to zero on its own.
analogy.breaks: A switch is only open or closed, and a lamp only on or off, but a bracket can take any value and two brackets that are not zero can multiply to any number, positive or negative. The circuit copies only the zero rule, not the multiplying.

practice.text:
- Get zero on one side by moving every term across, because the rule only splits a product that equals zero.
- Take out any common factor, x included, rather than dividing by x, so no root is lost.
- Factorise what is left into two brackets, as in lesson 2. If no whole-number pair works, lessons 4 and 5 find the roots another way, where there are any.
- Set each bracket to zero and solve each small equation.
- Put each root back into the original equation and check it makes both sides equal.

**Rule of thumb:** When x stands alone in a bracket, the root is the bracket’s number with its sign flipped, so x + 5 gives −5. A square equal to a positive number gives two roots of opposite sign, so x² = 16 gives ±4. A bracket that appears twice gives one root.

**Worked example:** In Calculus fundamentals, the volume of the open box cut from a 30 cm square sheet had slope 12x² − 240x + 900, where x is the side of each corner square in centimetres. The slope is zero when 12x² − 240x + 900 = 0. Every term divides by 12, which is never 0, so x² − 20x + 75 = 0. The pair must multiply to 75 and add to −20, so −5 and −15, giving (x − 5)(x − 15) = 0 and x = 5 or x = 15. Both check: 12 × 25 − 240 × 5 + 900 = 300 − 1,200 + 900 = 0, and 12 × 225 − 240 × 15 + 900 = 2,700 − 3,600 + 900 = 0. At 15 cm the cuts meet in the middle, since 30 − 2 × 15 = 0, so there is no box, and 5 cm is the cut that course found.

**Common mistakes**
- Splitting a product that is not zero, so x(x + 9) = −20 becomes x = −20 or x + 9 = −20. At x = −20 that makes 220. Take −20 across: x² + 9x + 20 = (x + 4)(x + 5) = 0, so x = −4 or x = −5.
- Dividing by x, so x² = 6x gives only x = 6. x = 0 works too, since 0 = 0.
- Taking one square root, so x² = 9 gives only x = 3. (−3)² is 9 as well.
- Keeping the bracket's sign, so (x + 2)(x + 5) = 0 gives 2 and 5. At x = 2 that makes 4 × 7 = 28.
- Stopping at the brackets. (x + 4)(x − 3) is the factorised form; the roots are −4 and 3.

checks.label: If the product of two numbers is zero then one or both of the numbers must be zero: on every screen set equal to 0, at every pointer setting the product bar reads 0 exactly where a bracket bar reads 0, and only there does the dot sit on the axis
The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola: every screen's curve falls to one lowest point and rises again on both sides of it, and is drawn whole once shown
Each picture draws its question's own equation: at every x from −30 to 30 in steps of 0.5, the brackets' product equals the value it is set to exactly when the question holds
Every puzzle accepts only its right answer: the right one names every root of its equation and nothing else, and each wrong one puts back a value that fails the equation or misses a root

The worked numbers: at x = 3 the bars read 1 and −2 and the product −2, the ends of screen 1 make 18, = 10 holds at x = 0 and x = 7 but x = 12 makes 70, the wrong picks make 28, 40, 28, 10, 66, 768, 8, 220, 52 and 2,400, the box's 5 and 15 make 0, and every line of working adds up

Before Check a puzzle draws no curve and its pointer sits off every root; after a right answer the curve is drawn whole and the pointer ends on the last root, where the dot meets the line its product is set equal to

Set equal to 10, the dot meets the dashed line at x = 0 and x = 7, where the brackets read −2 and −5, then 5 and 2, so neither is 10; with both brackets x − 3 the bars reach zero together at x = 3 only and the curve never goes below the axis
A bar is flat only where the value it shows is exactly 0: on every screen, at every pointer setting, any other value gets a bar at least 5 px tall on its own side of the zero line
A wrong pick whose value lies off the pointer's line says so, and leaves the pointer where it opened
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: Two dossier rules overreach: "opposite sign, so x + 5 gives −5" gives the wrong root for brackets like 2x + 5 (−2.5); "a square gives two roots" fails for x² = 0 (one) and x² = −16 (none); and the factorising step does not say some quadratics have no whole-number pair, as explain does.

"A parabola carries on rising either side" is false for upside-down parabolas (i6: a’s sign; i7: a thrown ball); and a root passed between steps need not change the product’s sign, as the touching root on screen 11 shows.
